steps.answer: The catalog returned only modern histories of mechanical refrigeration, and my searches found no pre-1929 public-domain texts on household iceboxes, springhouses, or cellars, so this answer is thin. The one period source I read, the 1914 bulletin Air Cooled Apple Storage Houses, says mountain growers kept apples in various kinds of cellars and caves that stayed almost as sound as cold-storage fruit (Air Cooled Apple Storage Houses, scan p. 3). The same bulletin says mechanical refrigeration was beyond the average farmer and that ice-cooled storage houses were usually impracticable except through cooperatives (Air Cooled Apple Storage Houses, scan p. 2), so cellars and air-cooled buildings were the realistic options for many. That source concerns orchard fruit in 1914, not kitchens, and its methods are dated. For the broader story, start with Frostbite (2024) and Refrigeration in America (1953), which cover what came before and after mechanical cooling.
